newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar climbs to four-year high against yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar climbs to four-year high against yen.

text.p: The dollar jumped to a four-year high of 125 Japanese yen on Monday, buoyed by higher U.S. interest rates and supportive words last week from Washington's treasury secretary.

In other Japanese markets, export-orientated shares rose because of the yen's decline but the overall market closed lower. Japanese government bond futures rose on the back of the weaker stock market.
The dollar hit 125.00 yen in early afternoon trade in Tokyo, its highest level since February 2, 1993, when it traded at 125.25 yen.
It fell back to 124.65 yen in late trading after the head of Japan's main business group said that the dollar's rise to 125 yen was excessive.

The rise came even though Japan's current account figures for February, released on Monday morning, showed its trade surplus rising, something likely to stir up fresh trade friction with the United States.
The surplus in the current account, which measures trade in goods and services, rose 15.4 percent to 865.2 billion yen ($6.92 billion) in February from a year ago.
A weaker yen is likely to worsen the trade imbalance since it makes Japanese exports even more competitive abroad.
"The market largely shrugged off the current account data and everyone is buying dollars," said a dealer at a European bank in Tokyo.

Currency traders said that there was strong underlying demand for the dollar, especially after the release of U.S. employment data on Friday that pointed to a possible further rise in U.S. interest rates.

"More of the large Japanese accounts are thinking we could go above 125 yen now and that the high for this week could be from 125.50 to 126.50 yen," said Ken Landon, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo.
The buying was also sparked in part by remarks on Friday by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who said on a visit to Tokyo that exchange rates should not be used as a trade tool.
Traders took the statement to mean that Washington still favoured a strong dollar. The U.S. currency has risen from a post-war low of just under 80 yen in the spring of 1995.

Investor demand was also boosted by the prospect of a widening gap between U.S. and Japanese interest rates. Friday's job figures showed U.S. wage costs rising, fuelling speculation that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again, dealers said.
Interest rate gaps of 10-year government bonds between Japan and the United States have widened to around 4.8 percent from 4.35 percent before the Fed pushed up rates in late March.
Traders said there were rumours in the market that Japan's Ministry of Finance had contacted life insurers, which are big investors, and suggested that they not buy dollars.
There were also market rumours that the Bank of Japan was checking the dollar/yen rate, sometimes a precursor to intervention by the central bank. But no yen buying by the bank had been detected.

The weaker yen boosted export-oriented shares on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, but the overall market was dragged down by losses in the construction and banking sectors. The benchmark Nikkei average of 225 shares fell 144.92 points, or 0.81 percent, to close at 17,715.67.
Bond futures rose on the back of weaker shares. The benchmark June contract rose 0.32 at 127.19.
